summary: Describes ISATAP, which connects dual-stack IPv6/IPv4 nodes across an IPv4 network by treating the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6. It provides automatic tunneling similar to a non-broadcast multiple access model. It replaces RFC 4214. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine carrying a letter in a new language through a country that only understands the old one, by tucking it into an old-style envelope. ISATAP does that for IPv6.

questions: ipv6 tunneling over ipv4 inside a site
how does isatap build an ipv6 address from ipv4
what is the potential router list in isatap
how does isatap tunnel ipv6 over ipv4
subtitle: Treat a site's IPv4 network as the link layer for IPv6, so dual-stack nodes can tunnel to each other automatically.

tldr.problem: Dual-stack (IPv6/IPv4) nodes inside a site often have only an IPv4 network between them, with no native IPv6 links.
tldr.mechanism: ISATAP builds an IPv6 interface identifier from a node's IPv4 address, so IPv6 packets can be tunneled in IPv4 automatically, and uses a Potential Router List to find routers.
tldr.outcome: It gives IPv6 neighbor discovery and tunneling over a site's IPv4 network, but only for sites that follow its security rules. It is Informational and replaces RFC 4214.

today: RFC 5214 is an Informational RFC and replaces RFC 4214. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What ISATAP Does
sections.content:
The Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP) connects dual-stack (IPv6/IPv4) nodes over IPv4 networks. Dual-stack nodes use it to tunnel IPv6 packets inside IPv4 automatically. In the RFC's words, ISATAP views the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6.

It works whether global or private IPv4 addresses are used, and it presents a Non-Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) abstraction similar to the one in RFC 2491, RFC 2492, RFC 2529 and RFC 3056.

The RFC limits its domain of applicability to automatic tunneling between ISATAP nodes within sites that observe its security considerations. That covers host-to-router, router-to-host and host-to-host tunneling in certain enterprise networks and 3GPP/3GPP2 wireless operator networks. Extensions beyond that are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A school has only old-style mail slots, but some kids want to send new-style notes. ISATAP wraps each new note in an old-style envelope so the school's mail system can carry it.

sections.title: ISATAP Addresses and Locators
sections.content:
An ISATAP interface identifier is built in Modified EUI-64 format. It joins the 24-bit IANA OUI (00-00-5E), the 8-bit value 0xFE, and a 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order. When the IPv4 address is known to be globally unique, the u bit is set to 1; otherwise it is 0.

Each ISATAP interface keeps a locator set: IPv4 address-to-interface mappings from a single site. The set MUST NOT span multiple sites. When an IPv4 address is removed, its locator SHOULD be removed; when a new one is assigned, the locator MAY be added. The interface forms link-local ISATAP addresses from the addresses in its locator set.

Because wide-area IPv4 multicast cannot be assumed, ISATAP assumes its IPv4 carrier network only has unicast capability. IPv6 multicast and Reserved IPv6 Subnet Anycast Addresses over ISATAP are not described.
sections.plainLanguage: Your IPv6 address contains your IPv4 address tucked inside it, like a house number written in a longer street address. That way anyone can work out where to send the envelope.

sections.title: Automatic Tunneling
sections.content:
ISATAP uses the basic tunneling mechanisms of RFC 4213. Mapping an ISATAP address to a link-layer address is a static computation: the last four octets are treated as an IPv4 address, so no lookup is needed.

ISATAP interfaces SHOULD treat ARP failures and persistent ICMPv4 errors as link-specific information that a path to a neighbor may have failed.

When an ISATAP node receives an IPv4 protocol 41 datagram that does not belong to a configured tunnel interface, it checks whether the IPv4 destination and arrival interface match a locator in an ISATAP interface's locator set. If so, the decapsulator MUST verify that the IPv4 source address is correct for the encapsulated IPv6 source. It is correct if the IPv6 source is an ISATAP address embedding that IPv4 source address, or if the IPv4 source is a member of the Potential Router List.
sections.plainLanguage: When an envelope arrives, the receiver checks that the return address on the outside matches the sender named on the note inside, or that it comes from a known router.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and the Potential Router List
sections.content:
ISATAP interfaces use the neighbor discovery mechanisms of RFC 4861, plus a few additions. The main one is the Potential Router List (PRL), a set of IPv4 addresses of routers' advertising ISATAP interfaces, each with an associated timer.

A node initializes the PRL from manual configuration, a DNS fully qualified domain name, a DHCPv4 vendor-specific option, or an unspecified alternate method. A new host variable, PrlRefreshInterval, sets the time between PRL refreshes; its default is 3600 seconds. When an FQDN is resolved with TTLs, the timer SHOULD be the smaller of that interval and the minimum TTL.

Router Solicitations are sent directly to a PRL entry rather than to a multicast group, and routers reply with Solicited Router Advertisements sent directly to the soliciting node. A received Router Advertisement is valid only if its source is a link-local ISATAP address embedding the IPv4 address of some PRL entry. Timers MUST be no less than MinRouterSolicitInterval, which has a conservative default (for example, 2 minutes).

ISATAP hosts SHOULD perform Neighbor Unreachability Detection. Routers MAY, but this might not scale in all environments.
sections.plainLanguage: A new computer keeps a short list of routers it trusts and asks them directly for directions, instead of shouting to the whole room.

sections.title: Site Administration and Security
sections.content:
Site administrators maintain the PRL, commonly as an FQDN in the site's name service. There are no mandatory naming rules, but the convention isatap.domainname (for example isatap.example.com) is encouraged. TTLs SHOULD be conservative to limit control traffic.

The RFC names two spoofing attacks: spurious protocol 41 packets injected from outside, and from inside by a node pretending to be a router. Outside injection is countered by site border routers doing IPv4 ingress filtering and protocol 41 filtering. For inside injection, administrators should keep the PRL up to date and make sure the resolution mechanism cannot be subverted.

IP security at both IPv4 and IPv6 levels should be avoided for efficiency reasons, but IPv4 security will not protect IPv6 traffic once it leaves the ISATAP domain, so implementing IPv6 security is required even if IPv4 security is available.
sections.plainLanguage: A site keeps a guest list of trusted routers, and the doorman at the edge turns away mail that was not invited.

fields.name: OUI bits (000000ug00000000)
fields.desc: First part of the 24-bit IANA OUI 00-00-5E; u is the universal/local bit, g the individual/group bit.

fields.name: OUI rest and 0xFE (0101111011111110)
fields.desc: Remainder of the OUI followed by the 8-bit value 0xFE.

fields.name: IPv4 address
fields.desc: The node's 32-bit IPv4 address in network byte order.
